answer_en: The work of a conversation designer is often confused with other roles, and the market currently lacks financial recognition for our profession.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: There's been a very recent pivot to user experience, interaction design and conversation design at my current company. That being said, the team is all very new and we are still trying to establish practical approaches to ways of working across the org (product, ops, engineering, marketing, design). Its an exciting time but it can feel like trying to move a glacier. I'd feel more clarity around growth opportunities if there wasn't so much opacity and confusion given the current state of the organization. I think I'd be more valued if there was a precedent to this kind of work here. The scalability of solutions is also still unknown as we are ramping up a new experience as a pilot with considerable tech hardware needs.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
1 - Today I see far fewer growth opportunities in the profession than a few years ago. I am disconnected from new opportunities, but talking to people who follow this closely, the perception is that opportunities, scale and growth are shrinking every day. With the mass adoption of generative technologies, this perception is reinforced by the business and its eternal goal of cutting costs and generating profit. My perception is that the use of automated tools to help less qualified people in the field is gaining ground.

2 - I would separate "my work" from the "need for this function" within the company where I work. My work may not have the necessary recognition for 2 reasons:
- Lack of indicators that contribute to this visibility (and when it comes to experience, this metric is much more challenging to measure in the short term)
- Management is business-driven (not experience-driven), so the viewpoint of those managing is never one of Design/conversation design process, but of "profit" and "costs".

In that sense, I don't think my specific work is valued, despite the recognition that undoubtedly exists.

On the other hand, and I believe the question is or should be about this, I understand that the role of conversation designers is well regarded and respected at the institution where I work. And the number of professionals involved, I believe, is above average.

3 - Regarding the last question, being just one among the 45-50 conversation designers at the institution, there is no possibility of my work causing significant impact with scalable solutions. Everything is already highly scaled; I joined when it was already moving. I just follow the established processes (even while identifying the many points of opportunity/problems). Changing something or developing a solution involves much more business and a whole team than my sole intention. And that is slow and almost demotivating in my scenario.

Understand the importance of UX writing, microscopy and its impact on the users.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
The conversation designer position needs to be positioned from another perspective. It is no longer just someone who designs a flow, but a key profile for the business. To achieve this, these profiles must be trained in topics such as data analysis and metrics, or even basic technical topics.
There is a serious hype problem where large companies seek to replace the work of the conversation designer with programmers or LLM technicians. That is why we CxDs have the mission to educate companies about what we do and the value we provide (customer insights, interaction design, research, etc.), which goes far beyond prompt engineering or asking an LLM provider to build an FAQ chatbot.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: I think there is still a lack of visibility of the work and awareness of it, even more so because very few of us do this. Personally, I might be the only person who is aware of it and trying to make the Conversation Designer role visible.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
1) Since resources are still scarse, not that much CxD focused conferences...etc, very hard to progress and grow if you don't have a mentor/ a colleague here to show you the rope. You're often thrown in a project alone. Action to achieve a 5:  Provide advanced training (multimodal design, and business strategy..etc) for those who want to grow without shifting into management.

2) While your contributions are appreciated within your organization, the client may not fully recognize the value of conversation design, possibly due to a lack of awareness or understanding of its impact. This can lead to challenges in securing buy-in for strategic decisions. 
Action to achieve a 5:
- Educate clients on the impact of good conversation design through case studies and measurable outcomes.
- Advocate for early involvement in decision-making processes to ensure the design is not treated as an afterthought.
- Work closely with stakeholders to align expectations and showcase the business value of a well-designed conversational experience.

3)
The current client lacks the necessary maturity in conversation design, which may lead to resistance to implementing scalable solutions. This can result in more tactical, short-term work rather than meaningful, long-lasting impact.

Actions to Achieve a 5:
Help the client build a roadmap for conversational AI maturity, showing incremental steps toward automation and improvement.
Offer workshops or training to educate them on best practices, frameworks, and long-term strategies.
Encourage experimentation with MVPs (Minimum Viable Products) to demonstrate the value of scalable solutions without overwhelming them.
themes: Education & mentoring; Role recognition & value; Team, resources & ownership

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Being able to create spaces for conversation so there are more options for shedding light on key topics.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Conversation design is often still seen as an afterthought behind integration and development or reduced to individual facets of conversation design, such as UX writing or bot personalities. With the current trajectory of agentic AI the whole field is also moving, kind of like the big vowel shift.
themes: GenAI impact on the role; Role recognition & value; Role scope & ambiguity

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Conversational communication is often left aside or underestimated, or, on the contrary, people expect it to magically solve the company's communication problems, which should be solved within a strategy with different communication channels, without putting all the weight on just one.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Right now I am not sure about growth opportunities in conversation design, mainly because the emergence of LLMs. I feel like I am being replaced. I know that LLM is one of the tool to design conversations too, but with prompting skills currently being the norm, I am honestly questioning the value and uniqueness of my skills and knowledge in the conversation design field. Maybe one of the actions/changes that could improve this is that companies must understand that using LLM fully as the main tool for conversations is not ideal. We still need rule-based dialog flows as well. And to properly design and utilize this static conversation flows, we need conversation designers.
themes: Career path & growth; GenAI impact on the role; Market demand & opportunities

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
This field changes so quickly and I've experienced some shifts in my role. I do feel pressured that I need to constantly learn and adapt to new technology to survive in this field.
Also, depending on the company's tech capability, the roles and responsibilities of a convo designer vary. Some companies don't have Gen AI capability and rely on traditional IVR/IVA platforms, which is fine. However, it does feel like I'm getting behind if I'm not working with the most cutting-edge conversational AI product. Regarding these, I hope there could be more conferences or workshops among convo designers addressing these issues.
themes: Education & mentoring; GenAI impact on the role

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
career growth: it seems to me that prompt engineering has taken over many cxd jobs, and so many of the people involved in gen ai prompting are clueless about the history and best practices of conversation design. I expect this will calm down, but currently it looks like conversation design is floundering and was replaced by gen ai prompting overnight (at least in the eyes of companies who are investing in ai products).

I'm not sure how to improve the other two right now...
themes: Career path & growth; GenAI impact on the role; Market demand & opportunities

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Budgets, customer vision, willingness to change.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: My organization doesn't provide any real mentorship or opportunity for growth.  As there are no other conversation designers, I'm basically given recurring tasks without the ability to improve processes or own strategy related to conversation design.
themes: Career path & growth; Education & mentoring; Market demand & opportunities

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: I don't have formal education in the field despite working in it for 6 years. Employers now can't seem to see past that. Really discouraging for immediate job change. I'll be getting my Masters, but options in that date also pretty limited

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
If I were interested in continuing my career working at large corporations I'd likely be more certain.
As a startup professional services business I am more reliant on and most influenced by my partners. With this in mind, my team is working diligently at forming strong relationships with potential partners which will help me achieve stronger results.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: I am not a conversation designer and none are employed by my company. They will not hire one in the near future even though we have several chat interfaces.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
1. The CxD role is starting to be understood and valued, but much more awareness is still needed beyond how to write good prompts.
2. The role of the CxAI designer in an organization often has to be fought for and justified, especially in projects that seem technical at first but always have an experience component.
3. Solutions are changing very fast, and although a large impact can be generated with scalable solutions, they need a good foundation that doesn't exist. There is a great need to raise the importance of transforming legacy systems into architectures that support the new advances in Gen AI.
themes: Career path & growth; GenAI impact on the role; Role recognition & value

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
CxD is still an emerging discipline for the general public and has to stand up against ""LLMs know how to talk" from the get go. 
Businesses make business because they do something specific in a specific way for a specific group, and unless we as the human race figure out a new way of communicating, conversations will be the ultimate bridging medium

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5

I’m happy to be an IC, and I’m already senior level. For now it’s just about honing my skills and knowledge, or figuring out what other work I could transition into.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: There aren’t a lot of opportunities for conversation design in my country so it makes it a bit hard sometimes and a few of the resources are costly. Also a lot of companies that provide scholarships for tech skills aren’t very aware of the conversation design space and it’ll be great to have more of that to help those who are interested in the field.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5

Educate. They believe everything can be done with AI.
I think we have the same problem as UX Researchers. There are many generalist roles that are absorbing content and research work.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: The company I work for is very large and highly structured. Although it has embarked on a good digital transformation path, it is unfortunately moving very slowly, mostly because of bureaucratic problems. It should offer more opportunities for professional growth, including attending webinars/courses abroad (outside [country]) given by professionals in the field. It should also take more into account the innovative proposals coming from Human-AI Conversation Designers.
themes: Career path & growth; Education & mentoring; Market demand & opportunities

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Market demand combined with a more defined understanding of what's involved in conversation design would help. It also would be helpful if the career progression from junior to senior levels was better defined. Right now, conversation design roles vary but they also overlap with other roles which causes tension instead of a sense of collaboration. I suspect this is because there is a lack of understanding across disciplines (often UX, strategy, and CxD) which leads to a lack of mutual respect and defensiveness.
themes: Market demand & opportunities; Role recognition & value; Role scope & ambiguity

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Well-defined processes, a holistic view of the user profile, brand reputation, seeing the bot as a channel with a specific goal within the company's overall objective, training, technical leveling, and sharing of cases for benchmarking.

answer_en: Better staffing / resourcing. Better understanding of what designers actually do, why our work matters, and why we have unique needs and struggles that aren't automatically shared with other roles like engineers etc.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Generally people end up pivoting to another concrete role, I'm now a Staff Product Manager building AI experiences. Conversation Design is important, yes but not enough to have a department as a whole it'll always be vertical under design and strategy. The intersection is so high that to build its own niche is difficult especially since with AI development everyone is doing everything
themes: Career path & growth; GenAI impact on the role; Team, resources & ownership

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
To reach or sustain a rating of 5, there would need to be greater awareness of the importance of Conversation Design for the product, both on the part of the business team and the company as a whole. In many companies there is still a lack of understanding of what Conversation Design is and what it is for, and this directly affects results. Investing in training and education in this area could be a significant change.

In addition, some companies recognize the need for this discipline but do not know how to apply it effectively. Providing a clear view of how Conversation Design can add value to the product and the user experience would help reach a higher rating.

My rating was influenced by the perception that, although there is growing recognition of the importance of this area, there is still a long way to go in terms of awareness and practical application.
themes: Education & mentoring; Role recognition & value; Team, resources & ownership

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: In the organization I'm currently contracting at, the engineers and product managers are creating conversational flows. So my manager and I are trying to make sure I get in front of all of the flows at least to review them.

For career growth opportunities, the rating reflects the availability of resources and mentorship in my role.

For work being valued, my contributions are acknowledged, but there's room for broader visibility within the organization.

For feeling challenged, while I work on meaningful projects, some tasks are repetitive, and the scope could expand to make a more significant impact.

answer_en: Business and product lack of understanding that the value of including and prioritizing conversational design benefits not just the user with a more frictionless UX but the bottom line as well. Much of our work is about reproving our value, and often we are asked way too late in the project process to contribute. Poor business-based short-sighted decisions supersede UX meaningful solutioning.

answer_en: Based on my current role and from interviewing - more visual product teams are experimenting with conversational AI, adding it on with the help of an LLM like OpenAI to get on the hype. This means I am managed by a very visual UI based User Experience team and a head of design who is more into brand uplifts and marketing style than UX issues. In future I would steer clear or any bolt on conversational AI departments and stick with chat first products like customer support automation or voice only interactions

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: I feel my work is valued, but there is still a challenge in getting leadership to understand the real impact of conversation design. Reducing cognitive effort in reading is often seen as simplistic, and the time needed to create a good experience is not always taken into account. A deeper understanding of the strategic role of conversation design beyond the text itself is still missing.

More work for conversation designers outside of customer service would help with feelings regarding meaningful impact. I'd like to see conversation designers take on new roles in industries like the medical field, education, news/sports media, and gaming.

answer_en: I do believe it is essential to make people (especially managers and directors) more comfortable with AI technology, in order to guide them and help them understand that AI isn’t a magic tool. The human component, the designer mindset, are paramount to design (and only then develop) truly useful AI solutions.

answer_en: With the rise of LLM-based solutions, many business and tech leaders see no use in conversation design because agents can now do that work. So in the past year, I've had to work twice as hard to educate people on what conversation design is, where it can and should fit into LLM solutions, and provide value beyond structured conversational flows.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Although the conversational role is more necessary than ever, our market value is determined by the companies that hire us or not. There is currently a tendency to abandon the conversation design layer because the new models solve the pain points that inexperienced eyes can see, and they consider that enough. Productivity is prioritized over experience.
themes: Market demand & opportunities; Role recognition & value

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: I do not see clear growth trajectories for conversation design. I don’t know what senior practitioners do after working 4+ years in the field besides writing books.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: Build organizational awareness; evangelize the importance of Conversational UX Design

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: I have spent a couple of years specializing in Conversational AI and, in my experience, the transition to AI solutions is only beginning.

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en:
I see an increasingly widespread perception, among makers of AI platforms, that their products are so sophisticated that conversation design and its purveyors are no longer necessary or relevant. Our presence implies that their products are not inherently PERFECT, and they deem this implication unacceptable. As a result, CD is treated as "optional at best", much like sprinkles on top a cupcake: to be added at the last minute, purely as decoration to the "real" treat: the AI-generated framework that is the cupcake.

The truth, of course, is that skilled CD is more critical than ever, in this Age of AI. But that is not the perception, which is resulting in a steady erosion of both our compensation and our reputation.
themes: Education & mentoring; GenAI impact on the role

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: I don't see that many jobs. if I ever want to leave a job, I am not sure I could, given what appears to be shortage of jobs. This is a big reason for rating career growth opportunities low. I am currently at a company that still tries to function like a startup even though we are beyond that stage in terms of size - as a consequence there is a lack of clear roles (everyone wears every hat), therefore even within my current job there's no real ladder to climb and achieve career growth.
themes: Career path & growth; Market demand & opportunities

question: Why this career rating / what would make it a 5
answer_en: CxDs report up through design which quickly moves up away from Conversational AI programs as one moves into management.

question: Definition of conversation design
answer_en: I explain that human conversation is like an interface that we use to exchange ideas between each other, and we create it naturally the same way we naturally learn how to use our bodies to walk. AI agents can also exchange ideas and accomplish goals for humans, but the conversation interface that allows humans and AI agents to communicate with each other must be designed and built, because an AI agent currently cannot create it naturally through learning. question: Definition of conversation design
answer_en:
Conversation design is a discipline that hybridizes several fields of knowledge, among them linguistics, psychology and computer science.
The goal of conversation design is to design conversational/dialogue flows that enable automated tools able to interact with users in natural language and help resolve the tasks the agent is called to perform.
Conversation design includes a purely humanistic part tied to copywriting (writing and defining the agent's communication style), a part that combines expertise in dialogue management (linguistics/psychology/psycholinguistics) and aims at designing fluid interaction trees, as well as skills related to the underlying technologies and therefore the limits and functionalities that can be exploited in dialogue.
themes: Dialogue flows & structure; Interdisciplinary practice; Language, writing & voice

question: Definition of conversation design
answer_en:
Conversation design is all about making AI chatbots and voice assistants feel natural, helpful, and easy to talk to. It’s like designing a really good customer service experience—just without a human on the other end. The goal is to make sure the bot understands what people are asking, responds in a way that makes sense, and actually helps them get what they need.

It’s not just about writing replies—it’s about creating a smooth back-and-forth flow, making sure the bot sounds like the brand, and handling things like misunderstandings or weird questions without frustrating the user. A good conversation design keeps people engaged, solves problems fast, and makes automation feel effortless instead of robotic.

At the end of the day, it’s about helping businesses talk to their customers in a way that’s smart, natural, and actually useful

question: Definition of conversation design
answer_en:
Conversation Design is the discipline of crafting effective, engaging, and natural interactions between humans and AI-driven conversational interfaces, such as chatbots and voice assistants. It involves a blend of user experience (UX) design, linguistics, psychology, and AI technology to ensure conversations feel intuitive and human-like.

At its core, conversation design focuses on:
	1.	Understanding User Needs – Researching user behavior, pain points, and expectations to design meaningful conversations.
	2.	Defining Bot Persona & Tone – Crafting a bot’s personality, tone, and style to align with brand identity and user demographics.
	3.	Structuring Dialogue Flows – Designing conversation paths that guide users smoothly toward their goals while handling errors and ambiguity effectively.
	4.	Applying Linguistic Principles – Using natural language principles to ensure clarity, coherence, and engagement in responses.
	5.	Ensuring Inclusivity & Accessibility – Designing conversations that accommodate diverse user needs, including different languages, accents, and accessibility requirements.
	6.	Leveraging AI & NLP – Understanding how Natural Language Processing (NLP) works to create training data, intents, and entities that enhance bot understanding.
	7.	Testing & Iteration – Continuously refining the conversation based on user feedback, analytics, and A/B testing.

Good conversation design minimizes friction, reduces user frustration, and enhances engagement, ultimately leading to higher satisfaction and improved business outcomes.

question: Why it matters
answer_en: Conversation design, when done well, ensures that a user-facing conversational interface/product is beneficial to human users and, by extension, the businesses to which the conversational product belongs. Conversational products are usually deployed by businesses with the goal of increasing revenue and/or decreasing costs. But the quality of the user experience (and how much it is improved over however users previously dealt with the task in question) is fundamental. If the conversational experience is worse than whatever preceded it, users won't adopt it at scale; perhaps they'll try it once or twice before giving up on it and forgetting it. The underlying technology can be as advanced as we'd like, but, in order for the conversational product to "move the needle" and have any significant business impact, users must use it and come back to use it over and over again. This requires a tremendous amount of investigation, planning, dialogue, coordination, design sense, and technical know-how. The best conversation designers are naturally inquisitive, research-inclined, design-minded, collaborative, tech savvy, and fierce advocates for human end users.

question: What conversation design isn't
answer_en:
Conversation design goes beyond simply drawing chatbot flows or writing automatic replies. It involves creating strategic interactions, always considering the user experience, business goals and usability best practices. The goal is to create efficient and natural communication adapted to the context of each interaction.

A common mistake I see is treating the conversation as a simple automated FAQ, without taking into account tone of voice, the user journey or context. Another frequent problem is creating very rigid dialogues that don't allow flexibility for different ways of responding or the user's real needs.

I also see a lack of accessibility in many chatbots, especially in journeys aimed at specific audiences, such as people aged 60+, who still face difficulties with technology. A good example is bots used in processes such as taking out payroll-deductible loans for retirees, where the solution needs to be accessible, simple and adapted to that audience. Many bots fail at this because they don't consider the characteristics and needs of the target audience.

In addition, it is crucial to dive into the client's business. Each brand needs a customized chatbot architecture, with AI or not. It makes no sense to adopt the same structure for all chatbots, even if they are in the same industry, such as automotive. Each situation requires a strategic adjustment that specifically serves the client and their audience.

answer_en:
One of the biggest mistakes people make about conversation design is thinking it’s just about writing chatbot replies. It’s not just about coming up with responses—it’s about designing a full, natural, and goal-driven conversation that actually helps users get what they need.

Another misconception is that a chatbot should sound overly human. While it’s great for AI to feel natural and friendly, trying too hard to mimic a human can backfire—especially if the bot can’t actually think, understand context deeply, or handle complex requests. The goal isn’t to trick people into thinking they’re talking to a human—it’s to create a smooth, efficient experience that makes interactions easier and faster.

People also assume that chatbots can work perfectly right away without testing. In reality, good conversation design requires iteration—analyzing real interactions, improving responses, and fine-tuning the chatbot based on what users actually need. A poorly designed chatbot that gives generic, unhelpful answers does more harm than good.

At the end of the day, conversation design isn’t just about automating replies—it’s about creating a thoughtful, useful, and seamless experience that makes AI a real asset to a business.

question: What conversation design isn't
answer_en:
Conversation design has a lot of powerful tools - entities, intents, LLMs, and words.  However, conversation design is not just any one of those tools.  For example, an LLM can have a conversation with something, but that doesn't mean it's a good conversation.  Words are predictable, but users responses to them are not necessarily predictable.  Conversation design is about understanding the choices, possibilities, and tradeoffs when attempting to solve a problem with a conversational interface.

Also, conversation design is not a one-off thing.  It requires careful monitoring and iteration to improve the effectiveness of the conversational experiences for users and new cases.

question: What conversation design isn't
answer_en: Conversation design is the art and science of designing interactions between humans and machines through natural language, both text and voice. It is not just about writing answers for chatbots or voice assistants, but about creating fluid, useful and intuitive experiences, respecting the dynamics of a natural conversation. Many people think it is only a matter of writing, or that integrating a chatbot is enough to have good design. In reality, it is a complex process involving UX design, artificial intelligence, linguistics, psychology and data analysis. Good conversation design is not limited to responding but anticipates needs, handles errors and guides the user naturally and without frustration.

answer_en:
1. Just writing words. Companies often think they can just release a chatbot or conversational experience and they don't need to do anything else, but they don't realize the work is only beginning when the experience is launched. question: What conversation design isn't
answer_en:
In my opinion, conversation design is not just writing nice dialogues or "talking like a bot". Nor is it simply slapping a friendly copy on an automated interface. Many people confuse it with just UX writing or with technical development, when in reality it is a strategic practice that involves research, experience design, personality definition, conversational logic, and deep understanding of the context of use.

A common mistake is thinking that any chatbot is the result of conversation design. But if there is no intention behind it, if it wasn't designed with the user, their language, emotions and goals in mind, it is not design: it is just automation.

question: What conversation design isn't
answer_en: Conversation design isn’t just writing chatbot scripts or clever prompts — it’s a strategic process that blends UX, linguistics, and AI to create seamless, intuitive interactions. The biggest misconception is that “anyone who can write can do conversation design,” but without understanding user intent, error management, and system behavior, even the best-written responses will lead to frustrating experiences. Great conversation design is about designing how a system responds, not just what it says.

question: Why these tools matter
answer_en: Most purpose-built design tools in conversational AI are development tools, no matter what the purveyors say. What conversation designers need to support a proper design process are lightweight tools that allow them to focus solely on the interaction they're creating. Any tool that forces the user to decide if they want a script node or an entity, for example, before dropping a shape on a page, is by definition forcing that designer away from the interaction and into the technology. To be clear: designs have to represent interactions that the technology can support, but you don't achieve that by introducing technical decisions in at the earliest design phase.

question: Biggest challenge of 2024
answer_en: The disruption from LLMs and RAGs, and separating out the facts from the hype with their adoption. There's a largely held assumption that LLMs "know" and have intuition, and that's not the case. They are probability machines, trained on data scraped from every corner of the internet. There's tremendous opportunity but also tremendous risk in adopting these tools. I feel like there needs to be much more clarity and education across disciplines to articulate when, how and if these tools should be use for specific use cases. Assumptions need to be challenged and companies pushing these products need to be accountable beyond the hype/marketing speak they're pushing.

question: Biggest challenge of 2024
answer_en:
The biggest challenge is being heard above all the noise that is being generated around AI. There's a lot of inexperienced and self-proclaimed experts who are trying to get a piece of the "AI pie" who are great at getting attention and clients but aren't delivering on their promises or work.  There's a lot of big consultancies who claim expertise but truly don't have a foundation of knowledge. The result is a knock on the credibility and value of conversational AI that means the genuine practitioners and experts have a bigger uphill climb because of a negative perception that often isn't warranted. 

We also have to figure out how to stop allowing the software/technology side of things drive awareness and evangelization because often those products present creating chatbots as "fast and easy" and truthfully, good experiences require time, resources, and knowledge so they aren't fast and easy. The result is a lot of organizations creating bad experiences that could have been avoided.

question: Biggest challenge of 2024
answer_en:
The biggest challenge faced by conversation designers in 2024 was balancing Generative AI capabilities with structured, reliable user experiences. While GenAI offered unprecedented flexibility in handling open-ended conversations, it also introduced new hurdles:
	1.	Control vs. Creativity – Traditional intent-based chatbots relied on structured flows, ensuring predictable and reliable interactions. With GenAI, responses became more dynamic, but designers had to ensure they remained accurate, on-brand, and aligned with business goals without veering into hallucinations.
	2.	Maintaining Consistency in Persona & Tone – GenAI models could generate varied responses, making it challenging to maintain consistent bot personality, tone, and style across conversations. Designers had to fine-tune prompts, create guardrails, and implement style guidelines to ensure the bot stayed true to its intended voice.
	3.	Reducing Hallucinations & Misinformation – Unlike traditional bots that followed predefined scripts, GenAI often fabricated responses when uncertain. Conversation designers had to find ways to limit hallucinations using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), controlled prompt engineering, and fallback strategies.
	4.	Ensuring Ethical & Responsible AI Use – With increasing scrutiny on AI biases and misinformation, designers had to be proactive in removing biases, ensuring fairness, and making AI interactions transparent. This included handling sensitive topics, data privacy, and regulatory compliance.
	5.	Seamless Handovers & Escalations – Many enterprises still relied on hybrid AI-human support models. Designers had to ensure smooth transitions between AI and live agents while maintaining context and reducing user frustration.
	6.	Scalability Across Channels – As users interacted with bots on multiple platforms (chat, voice, social media, etc.), designers had to create adaptable conversation flows that worked across modalities while optimizing for platform-specific nuances.
	7.	Redefining Metrics & Success Criteria – Traditional chatbot KPIs (containment rate, intent accuracy, etc.) needed to be re-evaluated in GenAI-driven bots. Designers had to establish new measurement frameworks to assess effectiveness beyond containment, focusing on engagement, relevance, and user satisfaction.

In short, 2024 was the year when conversation designers had to evolve from scripting rigid bot dialogues to orchestrating flexible, yet controlled AI interactions—leveraging the power of GenAI while mitigating its risks.

For example, my first job in the industry was data tagging/annotation and sample sentence creation. That role doesn't exist anymore because people will ask gen AI to "give me a list of samples". Clients are now starting to use generative AI to answer user queries, so there's no need for me to design flows anymore. I am morally opposed to how the gen AI models were created (i.e. from stolen, copyrighted data) and I strongly dislike their "black box" behaviour and the loss of control when using them for conversational solutions to the point that I am now looking at leaving the industry. I feel like it's destroyed all the parts of my job that I most enjoyed (namely user journey mapping and optimisation). Also, the available platforms for conversational design have such a focus on Generative AI that their base features are all but useless/under-developed...
themes: Field recognition & growing demand; GenAI & LLM capabilities; Role replacement & job insecurity

question: Trends of 2024
answer_en:
Most Exciting Trends in Conversation Design (2024)
	1.	Mainstream Adoption of Generative AI in Conversational Interfaces
– The rise of GenAI-powered chatbots transformed conversation design from rigid intent-based flows to more fluid, contextual, and open-ended interactions.
– Designers gained new tools to dynamically generate responses, leading to more personalized and engaging user experiences.
	2.	Conversational Agents Becoming Multi-Modal
– The integration of text, voice, images, and even video into AI interactions made bots more versatile.
– AI assistants could now analyze documents, screenshots, and voice inputs to provide more intelligent and contextual responses.
	3.	Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for More Reliable AI Responses
– Instead of relying purely on model-generated responses, many companies adopted RAG techniques, ensuring bots pulled from verified sources and up-to-date knowledge bases.
– This helped reduce hallucinations while keeping responses dynamic.
	4.	Personalization & Context Awareness at Scale
– AI-driven chatbots became more personalized by remembering user history, preferences, and past interactions.
– Context retention across conversations helped create a more human-like and intuitive experience.
	5.	Enterprise Investment in AI Copilots & Assistive AI
– Businesses moved beyond basic chatbots to AI copilots that assisted employees in real-time decision-making.
– AI-powered customer service assistants helped human agents by providing real-time suggestions, summarizing conversations, and automating repetitive tasks.

Most Concerning Trends in Conversation Design (2024)
	1.	Unpredictability & Hallucinations in Generative AI Responses
– AI-generated responses weren’t always reliable, often fabricating information when knowledge gaps existed.
– Designers had to spend more time defining guardrails and testing edge cases to prevent misleading information.
	2.	Loss of Control Over Brand Voice & Persona Consistency
– While GenAI allowed for flexibility in responses, it also made persona consistency a challenge.
– Companies struggled to keep AI outputs aligned with brand identity, leading to unpredictable tone and style mismatches.
	3.	Increased Ethical & Privacy Concerns
– With more AI assistants collecting user data for personalization, concerns around data privacy, security, and compliance became more critical.
– Regulators began pushing for stricter AI governance, making designers more accountable for bias mitigation and responsible AI usage.
	4.	Struggles with Hybrid AI-Human Interactions
– While AI became more advanced, seamless handovers to human agents still faced friction.
– Many businesses underestimated the importance of a well-designed escalation process, frustrating users when AI failed to resolve complex issues.
	5.	Metrics & Success Measurement Lagging Behind AI Evolution
– Traditional chatbot success metrics (containment rate, intent accuracy, etc.) didn’t fully capture the effectiveness of GenAI-driven bots.
– Companies struggled to define new KPIs that measured the quality of conversations beyond automation rates.

Final Thoughts

2024 was a transformative year for conversation design—one where the discipline expanded beyond pre-scripted flows to more dynamic, AI-driven interactions. While GenAI unlocked new creative possibilities, it also introduced challenges around control, reliability, and ethics.

Going forward, conversation designers will need to master AI orchestration—balancing the flexibility of GenAI with structured guardrails and human oversight to create trustworthy, engaging, and effective AI interactions.
themes: Ethics, safety & quality risks; GenAI & LLM capabilities; More natural, personalized conversations

question: Survey feedback

question: Survey feedback
answer_en: Just an overall note. I've been a UX writer for a long time and feel like conversation design is the next frontier in UX writing. I'm really glad to have shifted into conversation design, and I feel like it's going to help in keeping me employable. However, my fear is that much like UX writing, it feels like "everyone thinks they can do it" because "they know how to write". Yet quality is an issue. I also kind of feel like I'm figuring out how to do things myself and there aren't a ton of standards (but this was also how UX writing felt when I started in 2012).
